title: Stop paying for empires
author: Brian Elliott
summary: Brian Elliott reports from a Charter Forum session with Syndio CEO Maria Colacurcio, where managers whose teams had doubled were asking HR to take away their manager premium. He names the problem the empire premium: pay and levels tied to headcount, budget and span rather than impact. AI has broken that logic, because layers are being cut and spans widened while every worker is now supervising agents without credit or pay, and Lenny's survey found 51% of tech workers worry about doing more for the same pay. Strong managers are leaving first, though managers also have an edge in AI work and will return as coaches rather than routers. Elliott points to dual-manager models such as a large tech company's and Telstra's, which separate people leadership from work leadership. He closes with three actions before the next comp cycle: strike headcount and budget from leveling guides, build expert tracks beyond engineering, and price people leadership on people outcomes.
points: The empire premium pays for the size of what someone controls rather than the impact of what they do, which forces unwilling people into management and rewards empire building.
AI-driven spans-and-layers mandates doubled direct reports while pay stayed flat, and everyone now supervises agents as unrecognized 'manager lights'.
Research cited from Kellogg finds individual contributors earn roughly 32% less at the bottom and 63% less at the top than managers at the same level, which also contributes to the gender pay gap.
Managers remain essential, accounting for 11 of the top 14 factors linked to whether AI users benefit at work, but their role shifts toward coaching.
Rewrite leveling guides without headcount, budget or span, extend expert tracks to every function, and tie manager pay to learning, team health and results.
quotes: Call it the empire premium: the decades-old habit, baked into almost every leveling guide visibly or invisibly, of paying people for the size of what they control (headcount, budget, span) rather than the impact of what they do.
That forces people into management who don’t want to be there and it rewards empire building more than leadership.
The manager who had six people and a premium woke up with twelve people and, in many cases, the same paycheck, “much to the chagrin of these managers,” as Maria put it.
Maria’s summary of the comp team’s predicament is the best line of the session: “You have to articulate what you value in the middle of changing what you value.

When Anthropic analyzed about 400,000 Claude Code sessions, managers had the highest verified success rate, slightly ahead of software engineers. Command of the domain mattered more than coding skills.
Managers are responsible for 11 of the top 14 factors that link to whether AI users benefit from using AI at work.
Both models pay for an outcome tied to leading people and teams, and ignore headcount. Measure what people deliver, and stop paying for the activity proxy.
Take your manager, director and VP criteria and strike every reference to headcount, budget, or span. What’s left is what you actually value and it’s not a good list you have work to do.
